title.en: Causes, course and results of World War I

text.en: On 28 June 1914 a young Serbian nationalist shot the heir to the Austrian throne in Sarajevo. Within weeks Europe was at war. The shot was only the spark - the fuel had been piling up for decades.

Long-term causes: militarism (an arms race), the alliance system, imperial rivalry for colonies and markets, and aggressive nationalism.
Europe was split into two camps: the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia).
The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.
Austria declared war on Serbia, Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria, and Britain joined when Germany invaded Belgium.
The war was fought on the Western Front in trenches, on the Eastern Front and at sea; new weapons such as machine guns, poison gas, tanks and submarines were used.
The entry of the United States in 1917 and Russia's withdrawal after the 1917 revolution changed the balance; the Allies won and an armistice was signed on 11 November 1918.
The Treaty of Versailles (1919) punished Germany with war guilt, loss of territory and reparations, and the League of Nations was formed to keep peace.

problem.en: Why is the assassination at Sarajevo called the immediate cause and not the only cause?

text.en: It triggered the declarations of war in July 1914.

why.en: It was the event that set things off.

text.en: But the alliance system turned a local quarrel into a general war.
Militarism and imperial rivalry had already built up tension, so war was likely.

prompt.en: List the causes of World War I and two results.

requiredIdeas.en: Treaty of Versailles and League of Nations

commonMisconceptions.en: Naming only Sarajevo as the cause

points.en: Long-term causes: militarism, alliances, imperialism, nationalism.
War ended with the armistice of 11 November 1918.
Versailles Treaty 1919; League of Nations formed.
